extracted.intended_audience: educated English readers, policymakers, clergy, and readers concerned with the political and moral implications of the French Revolution
extracted.subtask_description: An eighteenth-century political essay/polemic (excerpt from Reflections on the Revolution in France) addressing history, religion, property, and institutional reform in the context of the French Revolution. It provides normative judgments about proper uses of history, toleration, ecclesiastical reform, and the protection of property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not punish corporate bodies for historical acts of members
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporate bodies are immortal for the good of the members, but not for their punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid collective retaliation against nations or corporations for the misdeeds of some past individuals; punishment of a whole class for former crimes is unjust (example comparisons between English and French historical wrongs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use history to instruct, not to inflame parties
rubrics_metrics.description: History should draw the materials of future wisdom from the past errors and infirmities of mankind; it may, in perversion, serve for a magazine, furnishing offensive and defensive weapons for parties in church and state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not employ historical narrative to revive dissensions or to add fuel to civil fury; avoid theatrical representations of past atrocities intended to incite hatred or persecutory impulses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply remedies to the causes of evil, not merely to names or forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Wise men will apply their remedies to vices, not to names; to the causes of evil which are permanent, not to the occasional organs by which they act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional changes that only alter names or outward forms risk leaving the underlying vices intact or allowing them to reappear in new guises; focus reforms on enduring causes (ambition, pride, avarice, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid focusing on the shell of history; address underlying principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Seldom have two ages the same fashion in their pretexts, and the same modes of mischief... Whilst you are discussing fashion, the fashion is gone by. The very same vice assumes a new body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not be satisfied by dismantling visible trappings; recognize that wickedness transmigrates into new forms and requires principled remedies rather than symbolic victories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject collective retaliation for historical massacres or crimes
rubrics_metrics.description: It would be unjust to retaliate upon present Parisians the abominations and horrors of the St. Bartholomew massacre; hatred of past crimes should not justify punishing descendants or contemporaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Condemn past atrocities but avoid using them as rhetorical or political pretexts for persecuting current groups; theatrical re-enactments intended to inflame hatred are dangerous and hypocritical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice moderation and toleration toward clergy's infirmities
rubrics_metrics.description: I allow in clergymen ... some tenaciousness of opinion, some overflowings of zeal ... I am a man who have to deal with men, and who would not, through a violence of toleration, run into the greatest of all intolerance. I must bear with infirmities until they fester into crimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between human frailty and criminal conduct; reforms should tolerate minor professional faults and only punish when infirmities become crimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify sweeping allegations before condemning a class
rubrics_metrics.description: From the general style of your late publications ... one would be led to believe that your clergy in France were a sort of monsters ... But is this true?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate and gather evidence rather than accepting mass denunciations; avoid generalizing the vices of some to an entire order without fair inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Praise and encourage genuine improvements in institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: If there was ... a great abatement, rather than any increase of these vices, ... in common equity they ought to be praised, encouraged, and supported, in their departure from a spirit which disgraced their predecessors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and support genuine amelioration in behavior and institutions instead of punishing them for predecessors' faults; reward reform where due.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware that popular election of clergy may corrupt clerical character
rubrics_metrics.description: An elective clergy ... will drive out of the clerical profession all men of sobriety ... and will throw the whole direction of the public mind into the hands of a set of licentious, bold, crafty, factious, flattering wretches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional designs that turn clerical appointments into electioneering contests risk promoting unworthy candidates and undermining religious authority and learning; ensure qualifications and safeguards if altering appointment methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure qualifications for clerical office (doctrine and morals)
rubrics_metrics.description: The new lawgivers have not ascertained any thing whatsoever concerning their qualifications, relative either to doctrine or to morals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reorganizing ecclesiastical structures, specify doctrinal and moral qualifications for officeholders to prevent arbitrary or irreligious appointments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect prescription and property rights as foundations of civil society
rubrics_metrics.description: If prescription be once shaken, no species of property is secure ... the positive ascertainment of its limits, and its security from invasion, were among the causes for which civil society itself has been instituted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal doctrines like prescription that secure long-established possession are essential to property stability; undermining them endangers all property and social order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not allow legislative assemblies to violate property or impose fictitious currency
rubrics_metrics.description: This legislative assembly of a free nation sits, not for the security, but for the destruction of property ... they have ... compelled all men ... to accept as perfect payment ... the symbols of their speculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislatures should refrain from confiscatory or arbitrary monetary measures that substitute fictitious tender for real property and thereby wreck commerce and confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oppose fanaticism and atheistical propaganda that destroy moral sentiments
rubrics_metrics.description: A multitude of writings ... and sermons ... have filled the populace with a black and savage atrocity of mind, which supersedes in them the common feelings of nature, as well as all sentiments of morality and religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combat the spread of writings and sermons that incite fanaticism or atheism if they undermine common moral feelings and civic stability; be wary of proselytizing societies that spread disruptive doctrines abroad.

rubrics_metrics.name: True toleration is respect, not contempt
rubrics_metrics.description: Those persons should tolerate all opinions, who think none to be of estimation, is a matter of small merit. Equal neglect is not impartial kindness. The species of benevolence which arises from contempt, is no true charity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genuine toleration respects the value of differing religious doctrines and seeks to protect the common principles they share (justice, mercy), rather than indifferent contempt for religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious reform must include justice and restitution, not sacrilege
rubrics_metrics.description: Sacrilege is no part of their doctrine of good works ... if your professors are admitted to their communion, they must carefully conceal their doctrine of the lawfulness of the proscription of innocent men; and that they must make restitution of all stolen goods whatsoever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious movements claiming reform should reject sacrilege and require restitution and justice; reforms that tolerate theft or proscription are not genuine religious virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious of substituting 'civic education' for religion
rubrics_metrics.description: They avow ... that a state can subsist without any religion better than with one; and that they are able to supply the place of any good which may be in it, by a project ... named a Civic Education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skeptically evaluate projects that aim to replace religion with a civic education founded on enlightened self-interest, as such designs may be used to erode religious institutions and shared moral frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of injustice matters more than which persons are first affected
rubrics_metrics.description: The reason applies, and it goes a great way. The long parliament confiscated the lands of deans and chapters in England on the same ideas upon which your Assembly set to sale the lands of the monastic orders. But it is in the principle of injustice that the danger lies, and not in the description of persons on whom it is first exercised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticize and resist confiscatory or unjust acts on principle, regardless of whether the initial victims are unpopular or belong to an adversary group.
